text: Done

. Report attached, task set to `needs_review`.

## What I found

**Four overlapping layers apply, not one.** Only three states have

a dedicated biometric statute, and only Illinois has a private right of action — but two other private rights of action exist by side doors that are easy to miss.

**The three states

that should drive your launch decision:**

- **Illinois (BIPA)** — the only true class-action jurisdiction. No injury needed beyond the stat

utory violation itself, so a defective consent screen *is* the whole cause of action. But the math is now bounded: the 2024 amendment capped recovery at one violation per person per method, and the Seventh Circuit held

in **April 2026** that this applies retroactively. Plan on **$300–500/Illinois user** worst case.
- **Texas (CUBI)** — no private suits at
all, yet the largest biometric recoveries in US history: Meta $1.4B, Google $1.375B. $25k/violation, no cap, AG aggregates across all users and

counts capture and storage separately.
- **Washington** — the finding I'd flag hardest. Its biometric statute is AG-only, so Washington gets written up as safe almost everywhere. But **

My Health My Data treats biometric data as "consumer health data," enforceable through the state Consumer Protection Act — a real private right of action.** Biometric data is enumerated there with no qualification as to use, and the first class action (

Feb 2025) alleged exactly your fact pattern.

**Two pieces of good news.** I opened by flagging your subscription as a possible BIPA §15(c) "profiting" def

ect — the case law substantially clears it, because courts require profiting from *the individual's* biometric data, not general revenue from a product with biometric features. Keep the scan outside the paywall and you

're fine. Portland's ordinance also has a "user verification on your own device" exception that fits you almost exactly.

**The highest-leverage move isn't legal, it's architectural.** Match-and-discard instead of storing a facepr
int collapses most of the report: BIPA's "purpose satisfied" trigger fires immediately, you get a real argument for falling outside Washington RCW 19.375 entirely, you satisfy Maryland's "

strictly necessary" test, and you delete the asset that generates the class action.

**Also worth 30 minutes today:** most carriers added biometric exclusions after the BIPA settlements. A policy covering actual-but-not-liquidated dam

ages is nearly worthless against BIPA. Exact broker questions are in that subtask.

## Two things to know about the handoff

**A housekeeping failure on
my side:** five of the original scoping subtasks (Tier 2, Tier 3, Tier 4, Build the matrix, Name the dangerous states) are still showing open because I lost their IDs mid-run and couldn't close them.

All the work is delivered — Tier 2/3/4 findings are in three "Findings:" subtasks, and the matrix and risk ranking are in the report — but you'll need to close those five manually.

**And the real

caveat:** this is research, not legal advice. The two states that can generate existential numbers both turn on fact-specific judgments I can't make for you. I'd treat counsel sign-off as a hard launch gate —
§6 of the report lists the six specific questions to ask, so you're not paying someone to answer "are we compliant?"
